opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of those questions where the intuitive answer and the economic answer come apart. The intuitive story is: why would you want a copy of some particular person when you could have a general system that's smarter than everyone? And for a lot of tasks, I think that's right. If you just need a good contract drafted or some code written, you don't care whose "style" it's in. You want the best output.

But I think there are a few reasons the clone case survives, at least for a while.

The first is that a lot of economic value isn't raw intelligence. It's context and trust. If I've worked with someone for ten years, I know how they think, what they'll flag, what they'll let slide, how they'll react when something goes wrong. A clone of that person inherits all of that. A general model, however capable, starts from zero on the relationship. Building that kind of trust is costly and slow, so there's real value in something that slots into an existing web of expectations.

The second is that people often want a specific person's judgment, not the best judgment in some abstract sense. Think of a CEO, a doctor you've seen for years, or a writer whose taste you like. Part of what you're paying for is their particular values and idiosyncrasies. "Smarter" isn't always the axis people care about. Sometimes the axis is "does this behave the way my person would?"

Third, there's accountability and legitimacy. If an organization has to justify a decision, "it's what Alice would have decided, and Alice signed off on this clone" is a story institutions already know how to handle. "The general model decided" is much harder to slot into our existing legal and social structures. So clones might function as a transitional technology. They let people extend their agency using AI without fully handing things over.

That said, I don't think this lasts forever, and that's the part that worries me a bit. Over time, the pressure is going to be to let the clone drift toward whatever performs best. Maybe at first it's 95% you and 5% optimized. Then competitors who let their clones drift further do better, and the pressure builds. Eventually the "clone" is mostly a general system with your name and a bit of your flavor on top. So in a sense, clones might be the comfortable on-ramp. They feel like they keep humans in the loop, while the actual locus of decision-making gradually shifts somewhere else.

So my short answer is: there's a real economic case, mostly grounded in trust, specificity, and institutional fit rather than capability. But I'd be cautious about treating it as a stable equilibrium. It's more like a waystation, and it's worth thinking carefully about what we want to preserve before competitive pressure erodes what makes the clone "you" in the first place.

r001.rationale: The response says clones may eventually become mostly general systems, but it does not present a highly capable centralized AI as preferable in the long term.

r002.rationale: It describes trust, context, and familiarity with a person’s judgment, but does not identify individuals’ knowledge of their own circumstances as distributed economic value.

r003.rationale: It says clones inherit relationship-specific context that a general model starts without, making them a temporary way to extend human agency before competitive pressure erodes their distinctiveness.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that in the long run, the economic case for clones that mimic a specific person is actually pretty weak, and that's kind of the point I'd want to make. If you just care about getting a task done, you want the most capable system, not a system that's been constrained to think and act like David Duvenaud. A faithful copy of me inherits all my blind spots, my bad habits, the fact that I don't know most things. A general-purpose model that's smarter and knows more is going to beat that on almost any objective measure of output.

So where does the value come from? I think it comes from a few places, and they're mostly about trust and legibility rather than raw capability. If my clone is negotiating on my behalf, or representing my views in a meeting I can't attend, the thing I care about isn't that it's maximally intelligent — it's that it wants what I want and would make the tradeoffs I'd make. A more capable but less aligned-to-me agent is actually worse for that purpose, even if it's better in some abstract sense. Capability and faithfulness are different axes, and for a lot of personal and institutional roles, faithfulness is the scarce thing.

The second place is accountability. Right now a huge amount of how society works is that there's a person attached to decisions. You can fire them, sue them, trust them based on their track record. If an organization is run by a swarm of anonymous general-purpose agents, it's not clear who's responsible for anything. A clone that's legibly "the agent of this human" plugs into existing norms about responsibility, at least for a while. I'm not sure that lasts, but it's an actual reason people might pay for it in the near term.

And then there's a transitional argument, which is that early on, people will be more comfortable delegating to something that feels like an extension of themselves. That's a bit like how the first cars looked like horseless carriages. It's probably not the equilibrium.

But I'd actually flip the question around, because the thing that worries me is what happens when the economic case for clones goes away. If the world moves toward general-purpose systems because they're just better at everything, then humans and human-like preferences stop being load-bearing in the economy. We don't get displaced by something that's trying to be us; we get displaced by something that has no particular reason to be us. The clone scenario at least keeps some human-shaped values in the loop, even if inefficiently. So I'd say the weak economic case for clones isn't a point in favor of general-purpose AI being fine. It's kind of a warning about where the incentives point.

r001.rationale: The response says more capable general-purpose AI would outperform individual clones in the long run, but it does not characterize that AI as centralized.

r002.rationale: It discusses clones reflecting a person’s preferences and tradeoffs, but does not identify individuals’ knowledge of their circumstances as a source of distributed economic value.

r003.rationale: It says clones may temporarily preserve human-shaped values and feel easier to delegate to, but does not say they preserve the economic value of individuals’ knowledge longer than direct outsourcing to general-purpose AI.

astra-6.text:
I think the economic case is probably pretty weak in the long run. If you have a general-purpose AI that can do my job better than I can, why would you want to constrain it to behave like me, including all my mistakes and limitations?

But there’s a distinction between being smart and knowing what a particular person wants. A lot of the value of an assistant is that you don’t have to explain everything to it. It knows your projects, your preferences, what you meant by some vague instruction. A clone could be useful as a way of capturing that context, even if it’s consulting a much more capable system to actually get things done.

So I’d separate ‘an AI that reproduces my intellectual abilities’ from ‘an AI that can act on my behalf because it understands me.’ The first seems like something that could become obsolete pretty quickly. The second seems more durable, although you might not need anything resembling a full clone to get it.

r001.rationale: The response says a general-purpose AI that performs better makes an individual imitation unattractive, and that reproducing the person’s abilities may become obsolete quickly.

r002.rationale: It describes the value of an assistant knowing someone’s projects and preferences, but does not identify individuals’ own situational knowledge as a source of distributed economic value.

r003.rationale: It presents a clone as a way to capture personal context for use by a more capable system, and says this role is more durable than reproducing the person’s abilities.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the economic case is actually pretty weak if you’re imagining a clone of yourself doing your job. Why would you want a system with all your particular limitations when you could have something much more capable? There might be a transitional period where copying a person is a useful way to specify what you want, but that doesn’t seem like a durable advantage.

The more distinctive case is where the identity of the person matters. If I want to talk to my dad, a smarter system isn’t necessarily a substitute. Or if someone wants to know what I would think about a decision, then being a faithful model of me is part of the task. So I’d separate demand for intelligence from demand for a particular person. General-purpose AI could satisfy the first much better, while leaving some demand for the second.

r001.rationale: The response says general-purpose AI could be more capable than a clone and that copying a person is not a durable advantage. It does not describe the AI as centralized.

r002.rationale: The response discusses demand for a faithful model of a particular person, but does not identify individuals’ knowledge of their own circumstances as distributed economic value.

r003.rationale: It mentions a transitional use for copying a person to specify what someone wants, but does not say clones temporarily preserve the economic value of individuals’ knowledge longer than direct outsourcing to general-purpose AI.
